title: The Internet Standards Process -- Revision 3
summary: Documents how the Internet community standardizes protocols and procedures. It defines the maturity stages, what is needed to move a document between them, and the kinds of documents used. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: The Internet is built from protocols that many independent networks agree to use. RFC 2026 documents the process the Internet community follows to turn a draft specification into an approved standard: the stages a document passes through, the reviews and waiting periods, and the rules for appeals and for disclosing patents. It is itself a Best Current Practice, and later RFCs have updated parts of it.

subtitle: The rulebook for how an idea becomes an Internet Standard, from Proposed Standard to full Standard.

tldr.problem: The Internet is run by many independent networks that need common protocols, so the community needs a fair, open and predictable way to decide which specifications become standards.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2026 defines document types, three standards-track maturity levels (Proposed, Draft, Internet Standard), off-track levels, minimum waiting times, IESG review with a Last-Call, an appeals chain, and intellectual property rules.
tldr.outcome: It is published as Best Current Practice 9 and has been updated by many later RFCs, so it is the base document rather than the final word on today's process.

facts.label: Min. Last-Call
facts.value: 2 weeks (4 if not from a working group)

today: RFC 2026 is a Best Current Practice, and later RFCs have updated it, including RFC 6410 and RFC 9282. Read those alongside it, since details in this explainer may have been changed by them.

sections.title: What the Process Is For
sections.content:
RFC 2026 documents the process the Internet community uses to standardize protocols and procedures. The process is an activity of the Internet Society, run on behalf of the community by the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) and the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG). It covers all protocols, procedures and conventions used in or by the Internet, whether or not they are part of the TCP/IP suite; for protocols standardized by other organizations, the process normally applies to their use on the Internet, not to the protocol itself.

The memo states that an Internet Standard is a specification that is stable and well understood, technically competent, has multiple independent and interoperable implementations with substantial operational experience, enjoys significant public support, and is recognizably useful in some or all parts of the Internet. Its stated goals are technical excellence, prior implementation and testing, clear and easily understood documentation, openness and fairness, and timeliness.

The procedures are designed to be fair, open and objective, to reflect proven practice, and to be flexible. The memo notes a deliberate balance: technical competence, testing and open comment take time, while rapid development of networking technology demands timely standards. The process is intended to be as short and simple as possible without sacrificing technical excellence, thorough testing, or openness and fairness.
sections.plainLanguage: Independent networks only interconnect if they share the same protocols. This memo sets out the rules the community follows to decide which protocol documents deserve that trust, and the values those rules protect: good engineering, real-world testing, readable documentation, fair treatment of all participants, and speed.

sections.title: RFCs, Internet-Drafts and Specification Types
sections.content:
Each distinct version of a standards-related specification is published in the Request for Comments (RFC) series, the official publication channel, under the responsibility of the RFC Editor. When a specification is adopted as an Internet Standard it also receives an STD label; documents recording best current practice receive a BCP label. Either way the document keeps its RFC number. For standards-track specifications, the ASCII text version is the definitive reference and must be a complete and accurate specification, including all necessary diagrams.

While work is in progress, drafts live as Internet-Drafts in a replicated IETF directory. They have no formal status, are subject to change or removal at any time, and are removed if unchanged for more than six months without an IESG recommendation for publication. The memo warns in strong terms that an Internet-Draft must never be cited in a paper, report or Request for Proposal, and that a vendor must not claim compliance with one; referring to a forthcoming specification as "Work in Progress" is acceptable.

Specifications fall into two kinds. A Technical Specification (TS) describes a protocol, service, procedure, convention or format and states its scope. An Applicability Statement (AS) says how and under what circumstances one or more TSs apply to an Internet capability, and gives each a requirement level. An AS may not sit at a higher maturity level than any standards-track TS it relies on.
sections.plainLanguage: Work in progress is a draft that anyone can change or that may disappear; it is not a published specification and must not be cited as one. The finished, numbered RFC is the official record. Within that record, one document type describes how something works and another says when and where it must be used.

sections.title: The Maturity Levels
sections.content:
Specifications intended to become standards move through three maturity levels on the standards track. Entering the track at the first level requires a specific IESG action.

  • Proposed Standard is the entry level. A Proposed Standard is generally stable, has resolved known design choices, is believed to be well understood, has received significant community review, and appears valuable. Implementation and operational experience are usually not required, but are highly desirable, and the IESG may require them for specifications that materially affect the core protocols or may have significant operational impact. Implementors should treat Proposed Standards as immature: it is desirable to implement them to gain experience, but deploying them in a disruption-sensitive environment is not recommended.
  • Draft Standard requires at least two independent and interoperable implementations from different code bases, plus sufficient successful operational experience. Interoperable means functionally equivalent or interchangeable in the system where they are used. The two-implementation rule applies to all options and features: any option not demonstrated in two interoperable implementations must be removed before the specification can advance. The working group chair must document the qualifying implementations and the interoperation testing. A Draft Standard is normally treated as a final specification, and it is reasonable for vendors to deploy it even in disruption-sensitive environments.
  • Internet Standard requires significant implementation and successful operational experience, and is characterized by high technical maturity and a general belief that the protocol or service provides significant benefit to the Internet community. It is assigned an STD number while keeping its RFC number.

Specifications off the track carry one of three labels: Experimental (part of a research or development effort, published as an archival record), Informational (published for the general information of the community, not a consensus or recommendation), or Historic (superseded or otherwise considered obsolete). Experimental and Informational documents not from a working group go to the RFC Editor, which waits two weeks for comments and may refuse documents unrelated to Internet activity or below RFC standards; the RFC Editor refers documents that look like IETF work to the IESG, which may require a disclaimer if it still publishes them.
sections.plainLanguage: Each level demands stronger proof. At the first level a reviewed, stable draft is enough. The second level requires two separately written implementations that work together, with unused options removed. The top level requires significant real-world deployment. Documents that never enter this track are labeled Experimental, Informational or Historic instead.

sections.title: How a Standards Action Proceeds
sections.content:
A standards action — entering the track, advancing within it, or removing a specification from it — must be approved by the IESG. The memo stresses that objective criteria guide the IESG but there is no algorithmic guarantee of elevation; the IESG's experienced collective judgment of technical quality is an essential part of the decision.

An action begins when a specification is posted as an Internet-Draft, unless it is unchanged since RFC publication, and remains posted for at least two weeks so the community can review it. The responsible working group then recommends the action to its Area Director, or an individual recommends it directly to the IESG if no working group is involved. The IESG checks the criteria and the technical quality and clarity expected for the target level; for very important specifications it may commission an independent technical review.

The IESG then issues a Last-Call notice to the IETF Announce mailing list. Comments are accepted from anyone. The Last-Call lasts at least two weeks, or at least four weeks if the action was not initiated by a working group, and the IESG may extend it. The IESG is not bound by the originally recommended category: it may consider the document for a different one, issuing a new Last-Call if the change would raise the level. After the Last-Call the IESG decides and announces the result; if approved, the RFC Editor publishes the specification as an RFC.

Minimum times apply as the document advances: at least six months at Proposed Standard, and at least four months at Draft Standard or until at least one IETF meeting has occurred, whichever is later. If a specification stays at one level for twenty-four months, and every twelve months thereafter, the IESG must review the viability of the effort and the usefulness of the technology, and may continue it, keep the level, or move the specification to Historic. A new version of an established standard goes through the whole process again as if it were new, and retiring a standard to Historic uses the same Last-Call and notification procedures as any other standards action.
sections.plainLanguage: Every step is announced and open. A draft waits at least two weeks for review; a working group or an individual then asks the IESG to act; the IESG checks quality and announces a public Last-Call of at least two weeks; then it decides. Waiting periods at each level give people time to test and comment before the document moves on.

sections.title: Appeals and Variances
sections.content:
Disputes follow a defined chain. A person who disagrees with a working group recommendation must first discuss it with the working group's chairs, who may involve the whole group. Unresolved, the dispute goes to the Area Director for the working group's area, then to the IESG as a whole, then to the IAB. The IAB's decision is final on whether the standards procedures were followed and on all questions of technical merit.

Complaints about an IESG action follow a similar path: first the IESG Chair, then the IESG as a whole, which reports its review to the IETF; then an appeal to the IAB, which may annul the IESG decision and restore the prior situation, or recommend action, but may not pre-empt decisions only the IESG can make. Claims that the procedures themselves are inadequate go to the Internet Society Board of Trustees, whose decision is final on all aspects of the dispute. All appeals must describe the facts in detail and must be initiated within two months of the action becoming public; decisions must be made and communicated within a reasonable time, deliberately without a fixed maximum.

The BCP subseries records community consensus on practices, principles and IETF process itself. A BCP follows the same basic procedures as a standards-track document, including review and a Last-Call, but once the IESG approves it the process ends and it is published; it is not suited to the staged roll-in of the track and makes sense only as an immediate, full change. RFC 2026 is itself a BCP.

A one-time variance can excuse some requirements when the IESG determines the benefits to the community outweigh the costs, considering technical merit, alternatives, precedential effects, and how narrow a variance can be made. The proposal must be issued as an Internet-Draft and given an extended Last-Call of at least four weeks, and is published as a BCP if approved. Variances cannot lower any specified delay, or exempt any proposal from openness, fairness, consensus or record-keeping requirements; permanent changes require the normal BCP process.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone believes a decision was wrong, they can appeal it one step at a time: from the working group chairs up through the Area Director, the IESG and finally the IAB, whose ruling on process and technical merit is final. Appeals must start within two months. Separately, the IESG can grant a one-time exception to a requirement, but only after a long public comment period, and never for the core rules of openness and fairness.

sections.title: External Specifications and Open Records
sections.content:
Many standards bodies, including ANSI, ISO, IEEE and ITU-T, publish specifications similar to the memo's Technical Specifications. To avoid competing versions, the Internet community will not standardize a mere Internet version of an existing external specification unless an explicit cooperative arrangement exists. An Internet Standard TS or AS may incorporate an open external standard by reference (many Internet Standards reference the ANSI character set ASCII), preferably one available online. Proprietary specifications may be incorporated by reference if the proprietor meets the intellectual property rules, and the IESG should not favor one proprietary specification over technically equivalent competitors; if such a specification is not widely available, the IESG may ask for it to be published as an Informational RFC. A working group may also start from an external specification and develop it into an Internet specification, provided it was supplied under the intellectual property rules and change control has been conveyed to the IETF.

Each organization involved in developing and approving Internet Standards — the IETF, IESG, IAB, all IETF working groups and the Internet Society Board of Trustees — must publicly announce its standards activities early enough for interested parties to participate, and must keep a publicly accessible record: the organization's charter, complete minutes of meetings, archives of working group mailing lists, and all written contributions. The IETF Secretariat maintains the formal record, and removed Internet-Drafts are archived solely as a historical record.
sections.plainLanguage: When another body already publishes a good specification, the IETF uses it by reference instead of writing a competing copy. Everything the standards bodies do is announced in advance and written down in public records that anyone can consult.

sections.title: Intellectual Property and Security
sections.content:
Section 10 governs intellectual property rights. The stated intention is to benefit the Internet community and the public while respecting the legitimate rights of others. No contribution subject to any confidentiality requirement or dissemination restriction may be considered anywhere in the process. By submitting a contribution, a contributor grants the Internet Society and the IETF an unlimited, perpetual, non-exclusive, royalty-free, worldwide license to copy, publish and distribute it and to prepare derivative works, represents that known proprietary rights have been disclosed, and confirms there are no limits on those grants that are known to them. The Internet Society warrants that it will not inhibit open access to IETF documents licensed under these terms.

Where patents or other proprietary rights are known or claimed and brought to the IESG's attention, the IESG must not advance a standards-track specification without a note in the document about those rights. Where implementations are required for advancement, only implementations that have taken adequate steps to comply with the rights count toward the two-implementation requirement. The IETF Executive Director seeks a written assurance that any party will be able to implement under openly specified, reasonable, non-discriminatory terms; the IESG does not judge the validity or scope of claimed rights, and the two-independent-implementations rule is used as practical evidence that terms are reasonable. Standards-track documents must carry set notices: a statement that the IETF takes no position on claimed rights, an invitation to disclose any relevant rights, the Internet Society copyright and disclaimer, and, when rights are already known, a notice that the IETF has been notified.

The memo's own Security Considerations section is one sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: People who contribute give the community a free license to use their work and must disclose any patents they know about. If a patent is claimed on a standard, the document must say so, and the process tries to obtain a promise that anyone can implement it on fair terms. The process document itself says nothing about computer security.

viz.caption: MATURITY LEVELS ON AND OFF THE STANDARDS TRACK (RFC 2026, SECTION 4)

items.label: Proposed Standard
items.desc: Entry level: stable, reviewed and well understood, but treated as immature by implementors.

items.label: Draft Standard
items.desc: At least two independent, interoperable implementations; all options demonstrated or removed.

items.label: Internet Standard
items.desc: Significant implementation and operational experience; assigned an STD number.

items.label: Experimental
items.desc: Part of a research or development effort; an archival record, not a recommendation.

items.label: Informational
items.desc: Published for general information; does not represent community consensus.

items.label: Historic
items.desc: Superseded by a newer specification or otherwise considered obsolete.

viz.caption: A STANDARDS ACTION FROM DRAFT TO PUBLICATION (RFC 2026, SECTION 6.1)

messages.label: Recommend action to Area Director (or individual to IESG)
Check criteria, technical quality; optional independent review
Last-Call on IETF Announce (>= 2 weeks, or 4 if no working group)
Decision announced; if approved, instruct publication
Publish as RFC; remove from Internet-Drafts directory

items.title: Internet-Draft
items.text: At least two weeks posted before an action can be recommended.

items.title: Last-Call
items.text: At least two weeks, or four weeks if the action did not come from a working group.

items.title: Proposed Standard
items.text: At least six months at this level before advancing.

items.title: Draft Standard
items.text: At least four months, or until one IETF meeting has occurred, whichever is later.

items.title: Stalled specifications
items.text: After 24 months at one level the IESG reviews, then every 12 months.

items.title: Appeals
items.text: Must begin within two months of the action becoming public.
